summary: What if you gave an 8-year-old millions of dollars to build their own rocket and the responsibility of sending an astronaut into orbit or to the Moon? In ORBIT, every decision affects your crew. Designed in Scratch for budding scientists aged 7 to 12, our video game transforms real NASA data (Artemis, SLS, DONKI, and OSDR/RadLab) into a thrilling space engineering and survival challenge where every kilogram and every dollar counts. Before liftoff, the player takes on the role of mission commander and designs their rocket, balancing budget, weight, and vital systems to achieve escape velocity. During the journey, they face solar storms, eclipses, and critical maneuvers. When they fail, they don't get a simple "game over," but a clear scientific explanation of what happened. ORBIT turns complex space science into active learning, inspiring children to solve real-world problems like actual NASA engineers.
details:
PROJECT DETAILS

1. What does it do and how does it work?

ORBIT: Mission to Orbit and the Moon is an educational and interactive video game developed in Scratch that simulates real-world space engineering and survival decision-making to take a crew from Earth to orbit and the lunar surface.

Assuming the role of Mission Commander, the player progresses through four main phases:

  • Budget Management and Rocket Design: The player manages an initial budget of $100 million (where purchasing all upgrades exceeds $120 million) to allocate resources among Propulsion, Radiation Shielding, and Life Support, balancing the spacecraft's total mass to overcome Earth's gravity during liftoff.
  • Deep Space Transit and Space Weather: During the 4-day journey (384,400 km), the crew faces solar storms, eclipses, and unexpected events that test the chosen systems.
  • Lunar Braking and Insertion: The commander must reserve enough fuel to decelerate upon entering lunar gravity (1/6 of Earth's gravity) and execute a safe lunar landing.
  • Scientific Failure Diagnosis: If the mission fails due to excess weight, fuel depletion, excessive radiation, or oxygen loss, the game avoids a simple "Game Over" and displays an educational screen explaining the exact scientific cause of the issue so the player can redesign their strategy.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Active STEAM Learning: Fosters critical thinking and problem-solving in Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics, turning every mistake into an immediate learning opportunity.
  • Accessible Scientific Rigor: Introduces authentic concepts of orbital mechanics, thrust-to-weight ratio, space weather, and radiation protection based on real NASA missions.
  • Strategic Decision-Making: Demonstrates through hands-on practice that in space engineering, every kilogram and every dollar counts.
  • Universal and Free Access: Built in Scratch, it runs free of charge from any web browser or offline, featuring an intuitive interface specifically designed for children aged 7 to 12.

3. What do you hope to achieve? (Expected Impact)

ORBIT aims to democratize access to space engineering and spark scientific vocations in children aged 7 to 12, especially in communities with limited access to laboratories or advanced educational resources. Through this project, we hope to:

  • Inspire early interest in science, coding, and space exploration among new generations.
  • Promote equity in STEAM by offering a barrier-free experience that motivates girls and boys equally.
  • Transform screen time into an experimentation lab where players think and act like real NASA engineers.
  • Raise awareness about the real challenges of human deep-space exploration (such as the Artemis program) and the importance of scientific planning.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Programming Environment and Language: Scratch (visual block-based programming utilizing dynamic variables for budget, mass, thrust, radiation, and life support).
  • Visual Design and Graphic Assets: Illustrations, backgrounds, and interfaces adapted from and inspired by NASA vehicles and missions (Orion spacecraft and SLS rocket).
  • Official Scientific Data Sources: NASA Artemis Program, NASA Space Launch System (SLS), NASA Space Weather Database (DONKI), NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), RadLab (OSDR Radiation Dosimetry Database), and NASA Space Place.
  • Super Intelligence (SI) / AI Support: Google Gemini, transparently used as an assistant to translate complex astrophysics concepts into clear language for children aged 7 to 12, structure the mathematical balancing of game variables, and support the drafting of narrative dialogues. (Note: No SI-generated content uses, contains, or modifies any NASA logos or protected branding elements).

5. How is your project creative?

  • Turns complex science into playable mechanics: Translates real equations of thrust, mass, and radiation dosimetry into tactical decisions that are easy for elementary students to understand.
  • Reinvents failure through scientific feedback: Replaces the frustration of a traditional defeat screen with a personalized technical diagnosis that encourages iterative experimentation.
  • Eliminates the "single solution": By preventing players from buying every upgrade due to budget and weight limits, it challenges each player to design their own unique survival strategy.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Pedagogical Approach: Adapting space and orbital terminology into visual, clear, and motivating language for ages 7 to 12.
  • Scientific Accuracy: Backing every variable, obstacle, and diagnosis with official, open-access NASA databases.
  • Technological Accessibility: Choosing Scratch so any student, teacher, or family can play, analyze, and even remix the code without requiring expensive hardware or constant internet access.
  • Inclusion and Motivation: Although our team is deeply involved in the STEAM world, we noticed that many children—especially in underserved communities—perceive space science as something distant or overly difficult, while their interest in video games continues to grow. Inspired by our own passion for rockets, space exploration, and hands-on learning at our school, we designed ORBIT to bridge that gap, allowing any child to experiment without fear of making mistakes and discover that real science can be learned through play.

To facilitate judging, all technical documentation, game scripts, and supporting files are organized in our public Google Drive folder:
